interactions.label: In phenylketonuria, restricting dietary phenylalanine prevents brain damage, but

params.question: In phenylketonuria, restricting dietary phenylalanine prevents brain damage, but tyrosine must also be supplemented. Why is tyrosine supplementation necessary in these patients?

answers.text: Tyrosine is one of the nine essential amino acids and can never be synthesised by the body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tyrosine is normally a non-essential amino acid. The body synthesises it from phenylalanine — it only becomes indispensable when that conversion is blocked.

answers.text: Without phenylalanine hydroxylase, the body cannot convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, so tyrosine must come from the diet

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. In PKU this enzyme is deficient, so the body's sole internal source of tyrosine is lost, making dietary supplementation essential.

answers.text: Accumulated phenylalanine destroys tyrosine already present in the bloodstream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenylalanine does not destroy circulating tyrosine. The problem is one of failed synthesis — without the hydroxylase enzyme, tyrosine simply cannot be produced from phenylalanine.

answers.text: The low-phenylalanine diet also eliminates all dietary sources of tyrosine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a low-phenylalanine diet restricts protein intake, the core reason for supplementation is that endogenous tyrosine production is abolished, not that all dietary tyrosine is removed.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is that tyrosine is normally synthesised from phenylalanine via phenylalanine hydroxylase. In PKU this enzyme is absent, so the body cannot make its own tyrosine — it must come from the diet.

Exactly right. Tyrosine is normally non-essential because it is made from phenylalanine. PKU blocks this conversion, making external tyrosine essential for producing catecholamines, thyroid hormones, and melanin.

interactions.label: Collagen synthesis requires vitamin C to hydroxylate proline and lysine residues

params.question: Collagen synthesis requires vitamin C to hydroxylate proline and lysine residues. Which of the following best explains why vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing?

answers.text: Vitamin C deficiency prevents peptide bond formation between amino acids in the collagen chain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peptide bonds form during translation on ribosomes and do not require vitamin C. Vitamin C acts post-translationally, hydroxylating proline and lysine after the polypeptide chain is assembled.

answers.text: Without hydroxylation, the collagen triple helix is structurally weak and cannot maintain connective tissue integrity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine residues are essential for stable hydrogen bonding within the triple helix. Without vitamin C, collagen is fragile, leading to weakened vessel walls (bleeding gums) and impaired tissue repair (poor wound healing).

answers.text: Vitamin C deficiency converts Type I collagen into Type IV collagen, which cannot bear mechanical stress

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Collagen types are genetically determined, not altered by vitamin C availability. Type I and Type IV are encoded by different genes; vitamin C affects post-translational modification, not collagen type.

answers.text: Lack of vitamin C causes collagen to denature into unfolded polypeptide chains

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Denaturation is the loss of an already-formed three-dimensional structure. In scurvy, collagen is synthesised but never achieves full structural stability — the triple helix forms but remains abnormally fragile.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the role of vitamin C in collagen synthesis. It hydroxylates proline and lysine residues after the polypeptide chain is made, and these hydroxylated residues are essential for stabilising the collagen triple helix.

Well done. Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Without it, collagen chains cannot form a stable triple helix, explaining the vascular fragility and impaired wound healing of scurvy.

interactions.label: Pepsin is the master activator that converts all pancreatic zymogens into their

params.question: Pepsin is the master activator that converts all pancreatic zymogens into their active enzyme forms in the small intestine.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is indeed false. Trypsin, not pepsin, is the master activator of pancreatic zymogens. Pepsin works only in the stomach. In the duodenum, enterokinase activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which then converts the remaining zymogens into their active forms.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Trypsin, not pepsin, is the master activator. Enterokinase from the duodenal mucosa first activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidase. Pepsin acts only in the acidic environment of the stomach.

interactions.label: A male infant with Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia begins developing recurrent bact

params.question: A male infant with Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia begins developing recurrent bacterial infections at around 6 months of age, despite producing no antibodies of his own from birth. What best explains why infections were absent in the first few months of life?

answers.text: The infant's innate immune system fully compensated for the absent antibodies during the first six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While innate immunity provides some early defence, it cannot fully substitute for antibodies against encapsulated bacteria. The delayed onset is due to waning maternal antibodies, not innate immune compensation.

answers.text: Maternal IgM transferred through breast milk provided protection until six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IgM cannot cross the placenta and is not significantly absorbed from breast milk. The secretory antibody in breast milk is IgA; the antibody providing systemic passive immunity to neonates is IgG, which crossed the placenta before birth.

answers.text: Maternal IgG that crossed the placenta before birth provided passive immunity, which gradually declined

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IgG is the only immunoglobulin class that crosses the placenta. It provides passive immunity to the newborn, but is gradually catabolised over the first months of life. By about 6 months, maternal IgG is largely depleted — and in Bruton's, the infant's own B cells cannot take over.

answers.text: The infant's B cells produced normal antibodies initially but stopped functioning at six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia, B-cell maturation is blocked from birth due to defective Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK). These infants never produce their own antibodies at any stage.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key fact is that IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the newborn. In Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia, B-cell maturation is blocked from birth — once maternal IgG is depleted (~6 months), the infant has no antibody defence.

Exactly. IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, giving newborns passive protection. In Bruton's, this borrowed immunity is the only defence — once it wanes around 6 months, recurrent infections begin.

interactions.label: In carcinoid syndrome, a tumour diverts tryptophan towards excessive serotonin p

params.question: In carcinoid syndrome, a tumour diverts tryptophan towards excessive serotonin production. Why does this cause pellagra-like symptoms (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia)?

answers.text: Excess serotonin is directly toxic to the skin, gut mucosa, and central nervous system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While serotonin excess causes flushing and diarrhoea in carcinoid syndrome, the pellagra-like triad specifically results from niacin deficiency due to precursor diversion, not from direct serotonin toxicity.

answers.text: Serotonin inhibits the intestinal absorption of niacin from the diet

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serotonin does not block niacin absorption. The mechanism is diversion of the shared precursor — tryptophan — away from niacin synthesis and towards serotonin production.

answers.text: Diversion of tryptophan to serotonin depletes the precursor needed to synthesise niacin (vitamin B3)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tryptophan is the precursor for both serotonin and niacin. When the carcinoid tumour consumes most of the available tryptophan for serotonin production, insufficient tryptophan remains for niacin synthesis, resulting in the classic pellagra triad.

answers.text: The tumour secretes enzymes that directly degrade circulating niacin in the bloodstream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Carcinoid tumours do not secrete niacin-degrading enzymes. The deficiency arises because tryptophan, the metabolic precursor of niacin, is diverted towards excessive serotonin production by the tumour.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is precursor competition. Tryptophan is needed to make both serotonin and niacin. The carcinoid tumour consumes tryptophan for serotonin, leaving too little for niacin synthesis — hence the pellagra-like presentation.

Well done. This is a case of precursor competition — tryptophan feeds both the serotonin and niacin pathways. A carcinoid tumour's excessive serotonin production drains the tryptophan pool, causing secondary niacin deficiency and the pellagra triad.

interactions.label: A patient is brought to the emergency department after smoke inhalation. Despite

params.question: A patient is brought to the emergency department after smoke inhalation. Despite severe tissue hypoxia, the patient appears cherry-red rather than cyanotic. Which haemoglobin derivative explains this presentation?

answers.text: Methaemoglobin — iron oxidised to Fe³⁺, unable to carry oxygen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Methaemoglobinaemia produces chocolate-brown cyanosis that does not respond to supplemental oxygen, not a cherry-red colour. It is treated with intravenous methylene blue, which reduces Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺.

answers.text: Carboxyhaemoglobin — carbon monoxide bound to haemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with approximately 250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. This complex imparts a cherry-red colour to the skin despite severe tissue hypoxia. Treatment is 100% oxygen to displace CO.

answers.text: Haemoglobin S — polymerised sickle haemoglobin blocking capillaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sickle haemoglobin (HbS) causes vaso-occlusive crises under low-oxygen conditions but does not produce a cherry-red appearance. It results from a single amino acid substitution (Glu→Val) in the beta-globin chain.

answers.text: Foetal haemoglobin — elevated HbF with increased oxygen affinity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Foetal haemoglobin (HbF) has higher oxygen affinity due to weaker 2,3-BPG binding, aiding oxygen transfer across the placenta. It is normally replaced by HbA after birth and does not cause cherry-red skin.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cherry-red appearance with tissue hypoxia is the hallmark of carbon monoxide poisoning. CO binds haemoglobin 250 times more tightly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. Contrast this with methaemoglobin (Fe³⁺), which produces chocolate-brown cyanosis.

Exactly. Carboxyhaemoglobin from carbon monoxide poisoning produces the paradoxical cherry-red appearance despite tissue hypoxia. CO's 250-fold higher affinity than oxygen makes displacement difficult — 100% oxygen is the immediate treatment.
